prompt: What is the main reason to simulate a material before making it?

options.text: To choose which few candidates are worth the time and cost of making
options.why: Simulation is cheap compared with synthesis, so it is used to narrow a long list of ideas.

options.text: Because a simulation gives exactly the same answer as a measurement
options.why: Tempting because computed numbers look precise, but a simulation answers for the model you built, which may leave things out.

options.text: Because experiments are never useful
options.why: Tempting if you only think about cost, but experiments are still how predictions are checked.

hints: Think about the cost of making and testing each candidate.
A simulation is a cheap first filter. Ask which choice saves lab time without claiming to replace the lab.

prompt: Which part of an atom mainly decides how atoms bond and whether a material conducts electricity?

options.text: The electrons
options.why: The light electrons around the nuclei are what hold atoms together and carry current.

options.text: The nucleus alone
options.why: Tempting because the nucleus holds most of the mass, but the nuclei mostly stay put in a material.

options.text: The colour of the atom
options.why: Atoms are not coloured in this sense; colour of a material comes from how its electrons absorb light.

hints: Which part moves and rearranges when bonds form?
Bonding and conduction come from the lighter particles around each nucleus, not from the nucleus itself.

prompt: Why does simulating a material need quantum mechanics?

options.text: Electrons are too small and light to follow everyday rules for balls and springs
options.why: Their behaviour is described by quantum mechanics, so the calculation must use its rules.

options.text: Because atoms are made of light
options.why: Tempting because light can also be quantum, but the reason is the behaviour of electrons, not what atoms are made of.

options.text: Because computers can only do quantum calculations
options.why: The computer is ordinary. The physics being modelled is quantum.

hints: Which particle decides the material properties, and what rules does it follow?
Electrons are very small and light. Everyday rules for balls and springs fail for them, which is why a different theory is needed.

prompt: A relaxed structure comes out of a simulation. What is the most accurate way to describe it?

options.text: A prediction for the model you built, to be checked against experiment
options.why: It depends on the atoms, positions and approximations you chose.

options.text: A measurement of the real sample
options.why: Tempting because it looks like data, but no sample was measured.

options.text: Always wrong, so it should be ignored
options.why: Tempting after hearing about approximations, but a model can be informative when its limits are known.

hints: Where did the number come from?
A computed number belongs to the model you built. It is a prediction until someone compares it with a measurement.

prompt: A method costs size to the power 3. By what factor does the cost grow when the system size doubles?

options.why: Doubling multiplies the cost by 2 to the power 3, which is 8.
Tempting because 2 times 3 is 6, but a power means repeated multiplication, not multiplying by 3.
Tempting because the exponent is 3, but the factor is 2 raised to that exponent.

hints: Cost goes as N to the p. Compare (2N) to the p with N to the p.
Doubling gives (2N)^p / N^p = 2^p. Put p = 3 into that.

prompt: Which method uses no electrons in the calculation at all?

options.text: A force field
options.why: A force field uses fixed rules for the forces between atoms.

options.text: Hartree-Fock
options.why: Tempting because it is called a simple method, but it treats the electrons, only in an average way.

options.text: DFT
options.why: DFT works with the electron density, so electrons are included.

hints: Which rung has no electrons, only atoms pushing on atoms?
Names on the ladder: force fields, Hartree-Fock, coupled cluster, DFT. Only one of them skips electrons altogether.

prompt: The lab shows a straight line on a chart with both axes logarithmic. What does a steeper line mean?

options.text: The cost grows with a higher power of the size
options.why: On a log-log chart the steepness of a straight line is the exponent.

options.text: The method takes more seconds at every size
options.why: Tempting, but the lab plots relative cost with equal prefactors, not time.

options.text: The method is more accurate
options.why: Steepness is about cost growth, not accuracy.

hints: What does the slope of a line on a log-log chart measure?
A straight line on log-log axes means a power law. A larger exponent gives a steeper line.

prompt: What is the one approximate ingredient in practical DFT?

options.text: The exchange-correlation functional
options.why: The theory is exact in principle, and this one term must be approximated.

options.text: The idea of using the density
options.why: Tempting because the density sounds like a shortcut, but the theory shows it carries all ground-state information.

options.text: The laws of electrostatics
options.why: Electrostatics is treated exactly in the standard formulation.

hints: Which part of the energy has no known exact form?
DFT is exact in principle. Ask which single term in its energy has no exact formula.

prompt: The lab draws every curve starting at the same point. What does that let you conclude?

options.text: Nothing about which method is cheaper at a small size
options.why: All prefactors are set equal by construction, so only the steepness carries information.

options.text: That all methods cost the same for small systems
options.why: Tempting because the curves meet, but they meet by construction.

options.text: That DFT is the cheapest method in practice
options.why: The lab does not compare absolute costs.

hints: Read the "What to notice" box in the lab.
The lab sets every prefactor equal, so it shows relative cost. It says nothing about absolute run time at small sizes.

prompt: DFT is mainly a theory of which state?

options.text: The ground state, the lowest-energy arrangement of the electrons
options.why: The Hohenberg-Kohn theorem is a statement about the ground state.

options.text: Excited states, such as light absorption
options.why: Tempting because optical properties matter, but they go beyond the ground-state theory.

options.text: The state at high temperature
options.why: A standard calculation holds the nuclei still at zero temperature.

hints: Which state has the lowest energy?
DFT is built on the ground-state density, so it speaks about the lowest-energy arrangement of the electrons.

prompt: A band gap from a common functional disagrees with an experiment. What is the best first reading?

options.text: It may be a known limitation of the functional, so check which functional was used and compare with published results
options.why: Common functionals are known to underestimate gaps, which is why others exist.

options.text: Your VASP installation is certainly broken
options.why: Tempting because the gap looks wrong, but the disagreement is usually about the functional.

options.text: DFT has been proven useless
options.why: The limitation is specific and has known remedies.

hints: Where does the approximation sit in DFT?
Common approximate functionals are known to underestimate gaps. The first move is to check the functional, not to blame the software.

prompt: Which question is DFT not built to answer directly?

options.text: Exactly how a material absorbs light, which involves excited states
options.why: Ground-state theory says nothing directly about excited states.

options.text: Which of two structures has lower energy
options.why: Comparing ground-state energies is what DFT is good at.

options.text: What the forces on the atoms are
options.why: Forces come from the ground-state energy and are routinely computed.

hints: Does the question involve states above the ground state?
Absorbing light lifts an electron out of the ground state. Ground-state theory does not describe that directly.

prompt: Why should you report the functional with a computed band gap?

options.text: The number depends on it, so the result is incomplete without it
options.why: Different functionals can give different gaps for the same structure.

options.text: Because VASP refuses to run without a report
options.why: This is a matter of good practice, not a program requirement.

options.text: Because the functional only changes the file name
options.why: The functional changes the physics of the calculation.

hints: Where does the exchange-correlation approximation enter?
The band gap depends on which exchange-correlation approximation was used, so the number is incomplete without it.

prompt: What is a sensible order for learning?

options.text: A picture of the method, then practical choices, then checking your results
options.why: Each stage gives the vocabulary needed for the next.

options.text: Start with the largest model and a copied INCAR
options.why: Tempting because it looks fast, but failures in a large model are hard to read.

options.text: Skip straight to the band gap
options.why: A gap is only worth reading after the earlier steps were done and checked.

hints: Think about what each stage lets you understand next.
Each stage prepares the next: understand the idea, then make practical choices, then check results.

prompt: Which four files does a VASP calculation need?

options.text: POSCAR, KPOINTS, INCAR and POTCAR
options.why: Structure, k-point sampling, run settings and the electron-ion description.

options.text: OUTCAR, CONTCAR, WAVECAR and CHGCAR
options.why: Tempting because these are well-known files, but they are outputs.

options.text: INCAR and POSCAR only
options.why: Two more inputs are needed to run.

hints: Four inputs describe structure, sampling, settings and the atoms.
One file holds the structure, one the k-point sampling, one the settings, and one the description of each atom type.

prompt: Does this site run VASP for you?

options.text: No. It runs in your browser, and your files stay on your computer
options.why: VASP needs a licence and a computer to run on; the site runs no server.

options.text: Yes, upload your files and it runs them
options.why: Tempting for convenience, but no files are uploaded and no server exists.

options.text: Yes, but only for small cells
options.why: The site never runs VASP.

hints: Where does the computation on this site happen?
The site is a learning and tools site that runs in the browser. VASP itself is a licensed program you run elsewhere.

prompt: Your first project fails a few times. What is the right reading?

options.text: This is normal. Read the error messages and fix one thing at a time
options.why: Reading errors is a skill that builds with practice.

options.text: You are not suited to this
options.why: Tempting if you expect it to work first time, but early failures are common.

options.text: Copy a different INCAR until it runs
options.why: A run that starts is not a run you understand or can trust.

hints: What did the page say about the effort involved?
Early failures are expected. The page recommends reading messages and changing one thing at a time.

prompt: What does a word with a dotted underline in a topic page mean?

options.text: It is a defined term: hover, focus or click to read its short definition
options.why: The definition opens in place, so you do not lose your spot on the page.

options.text: It is a link that takes you away to another site
options.why: Tempting because underlines usually mean links, but a dotted underline opens the definition on the same page.

options.text: It is a spelling mistake in the text
options.why: Tempting because underlines mark errors in some editors, but here they mark defined terms.

hints: Think of the first time a new word appears.
The definition is short and appears without leaving the page.

prompt: Where do the VASP settings for a topic appear?

options.text: In the "In VASP" part, in a copyable block
options.why: Each topic ends its practical part with the settings that matter, in a block you can copy.

options.text: Only in the glossary
options.why: Tempting because the glossary defines terms, but settings belong to the topic page where they are used.

options.text: Only on the references page
options.why: Tempting because references name the VASP wiki, but the settings themselves sit in the topic.

hints: Look for the part named after the program.
It comes after the math part and before the part about what changes what.

prompt: What does the level switch change on a page?

options.text: How much depth you see, from the simplest correct version to full equations and edge cases
options.why: Higher levels add practical depth and the full math, without changing what is correct.

options.text: Which topic is shown
options.why: Tempting because levels sound like course choices, but the topic stays the same.

options.text: Whether the content is correct
options.why: Tempting because simple can sound wrong, but every level states a correct version of the idea.

hints: Beginner shows the simplest correct version.
Pro adds equations, edge cases and pointers to the literature.

prompt: Which three questions does each page answer about every setting?

options.text: Why you set it, why that value, and what happens if you skip it or get it wrong
options.why: This is the habit the site tries to build: knowing the reason, not only the value to copy.

options.text: Who invented it, when, and where
options.why: Tempting because history is interesting, but it does not help you choose a value.

options.text: How much it costs, how fast it runs, and who pays
options.why: Tempting because cost matters in practice, but these are not the three questions the pages answer.

hints: They are about reasons, not about history.
One of them is about what happens if you skip the setting.

prompt: In a material simulation, what is "the model"?

options.text: The atoms and positions you give the program: whatever you leave out, it does not know about
options.why: The program computes only for the structure you describe.

options.text: The real sample in the laboratory
options.why: Tempting because a model stands for the sample, but the model is the description you give the program.

options.text: The computer that runs the calculation
options.why: Tempting because the computer is the visible part, but the model is the description of the material.

hints: A wind tunnel tests a model aircraft, not the real one.
Think about what the program is actually given.

prompt: A real sample has a surface, but your model leaves it out. What follows?

options.text: The answer leaves out the effect of the surface too
options.why: A simulation answers for the model you built, not for the real sample.

options.text: The program adds the surface automatically
options.why: Tempting because the program seems smart, but it only knows what you describe.

options.text: The answer is still exact for the real sample
options.why: Tempting because the number looks precise, but precision is not the same as describing the right system.

hints: Recall the page on treating a result as a measurement.
What the model leaves out, the result leaves out.

prompt: What is a nucleus, compared with the electrons around it?

options.text: Tiny and heavy, and it mostly stays where it is
options.why: The electrons are lighter and are what hold the crowd of atoms together.

options.text: Light and fast, and it glues the atoms together
options.why: Tempting because the glue role is real, but it belongs to the electrons.

options.text: The same as an electron
options.why: Tempting because both are tiny, but the nucleus is far heavier.

hints: Think of a heavy centre with a light cloud around it.
Which of the two do the atoms share when they bond?

prompt: Which of these is decided mainly by the electrons of a material?

options.text: Which colours of light it absorbs
options.why: Electrons decide bonding, conduction and colour.

options.text: How many protons each nucleus has
options.why: Tempting because the nucleus matters, but the proton count defines the element and is part of the model you give.

options.text: The country where the sample was made
options.why: Tempting as a distractor, but where a sample was made has no effect on its electrons.

hints: The page names three things electrons decide: bonding, conduction and one more.
Which option is about light?

prompt: Why must a model say which kind each atom is?

options.text: Different atoms make a different material, so the energy and forces change
options.why: Changing the kind of atoms is changing the material.

options.text: Only to label the file
options.why: Tempting because labels look harmless, but the program uses the kind to decide how electrons behave.

options.text: The program guesses the material from the title
options.why: Tempting because the title is the first thing you write, but the program never guesses.

hints: See the "What changes what" table on the first page.
Think of swapping one element for another.

prompt: What does the Schrödinger equation connect, for the electrons of a material?

options.text: The Hamiltonian (the recipe of all the energies) with the wavefunction and the energy
options.why: Solving it would give the wavefunction of all the electrons together and the energy that goes with it.

options.text: The price of a calculation with its run time
options.why: Tempting because cost is a theme on the site, but that is the topic of scaling, not of this equation.

options.text: A ball on a spring with its speed
options.why: Tempting because the equation is old and general, but its job here is electrons, not balls and springs.

hints: The equation has three symbols: H, psi and E.
Recall what the wavefunction describes.

prompt: Can the Schrödinger equation be solved exactly for a material with many electrons?

options.text: No, so every practical method is an approximation of some kind
options.why: For more than a couple of electrons nobody can solve it exactly.

options.text: Yes, with a fast enough laptop
options.why: Tempting because computers keep getting faster, but the problem grows faster still.

options.text: Yes, but only for metals
options.why: Tempting because metals seem simple, but they are not exactly solvable either.

hints: The next page lines up the methods by cost.
What does the word "practical" imply about the method?

prompt: Why can the electrons be solved for with the nuclei held fixed?

options.text: The nuclei are heavy and slow, while the electrons are light and fast
options.why: This split is the Born-Oppenheimer approximation, which most calculations on this site rely on.

options.text: Because nuclei have no effect on electrons
options.why: Tempting because nuclei stay still, but they attract the electrons and are essential.

options.text: Because electrons are heavier than nuclei
options.why: Tempting by mixing up the two, but it is the other way round.

hints: Compare the masses of the two kinds of particle.
Slow and heavy versus light and fast.

prompt: Which statement about the ladder of methods is correct?

options.text: Higher rungs can be more accurate, and they cost much more
options.why: The ladder trades accuracy against cost.

options.text: Higher rungs are always faster
options.why: Tempting because newer sounds quicker, but the top rungs are the slowest.

options.text: Every rung gives the same answer
options.why: Tempting because all methods study the same material, but approximations differ.

hints: The picture is of rungs from rough and quick to accurate and slow.
There is no free lunch in the ladder.

prompt: A method costs size to the power 5. By what factor does the cost grow when the system size doubles?
hints: Doubling multiplies the cost by 2^p.
Compute 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2.

prompt: Why is a large scaling exponent a practical problem?

options.text: Each doubling of the system multiplies the cost by a big factor, so large systems become out of reach
options.why: Cost follows size to a power, so a bigger exponent grows far faster.

options.text: It makes the answer less accurate at every size
options.why: Tempting because expensive sounds like fussy, but scaling is about cost, not accuracy.

options.text: It only matters when the computer is old
options.why: Tempting because hardware matters, but a steep power outruns any realistic hardware gain.

hints: Compare 2^3 with 2^7.
The lab compares steepness, not heights.

prompt: A standard calculation holds the nuclei still at zero temperature. What does this mean for a question about heat and time?

options.text: A single ground-state calculation does not answer it, and extra steps are needed
options.why: Heat, motion and time are beyond one standard run.

options.text: It answers it directly
options.why: Tempting because the calculation is detailed, but it contains no time.

options.text: It answers it if you use a bigger cell
options.why: Tempting because bigger sounds better, but cell size does not add temperature.

hints: Look at the "not built for" list on the scope page.
What does zero temperature rule out?

prompt: What is the ground state of a set of atoms?

options.text: The arrangement of the electrons with the lowest energy
options.why: It is the lowest-energy state of the electrons for the given atoms.

options.text: The arrangement with the highest energy
options.why: Tempting by reversal, but ground means lowest.

options.text: The arrangement that appears at high temperature
options.why: Tempting because high temperature changes things, but the ground state is defined by energy, not temperature.

hints: Ground is the bottom.
Which option mentions the lowest energy?

prompt: Which of these is a ground-state question?

options.text: Which of two atomic arrangements has lower energy?
options.why: Comparing the lowest energies of two models is the typical DFT task.

options.text: Exactly how does the material absorb light?
options.why: Tempting because it is a natural question, but absorption involves excited states.

options.text: What happens to the sample over an hour of heating?
options.why: Tempting because it is practical, but it needs time and temperature.

hints: Which question asks only for energies of lowest-energy states?
Excited states and time are outside the ground-state theory.

prompt: What does the Hohenberg-Kohn theorem say determines everything about the ground state?

options.text: The ground-state electron density
options.why: The density, the amount of charge at each point, is enough.

options.text: The temperature of the sample
options.why: Tempting because temperature affects materials, but the theorem is about the density.

options.text: The colour of the material
options.why: Tempting because colour is visible, but it is a result and not the starting point.

hints: It is a map over space.
Recall the three-variable quantity from module 3.

prompt: In the author's five-step protocol for a first project, what comes first?

options.text: A relaxation: prepare the four input files and relax the structure
options.why: Relaxation comes first and later steps build on it.

options.text: Optical properties
options.why: Tempting because they are the goal for some, but they are the last step.

options.text: Elastic properties
options.why: Tempting because they are a headline result, but they come after the relaxation and SCF steps.

hints: You need a stable structure before you ask for properties.
The first step starts with the four input files.

prompt: Is the five-step protocol a universal recipe for every system?

options.text: No: metals, magnets and large cells may need different choices
options.why: It is a path for a first project, not a recipe for everything.

options.text: Yes, for every system
options.why: Tempting because a recipe is comforting, but systems differ.

options.text: Yes, but only for oxides
options.why: Tempting because the worked example is an oxide, but the rule is that the protocol is a starting path.

hints: The page calls it a path for a first project.
What do convergence and common-errors pages collect?

prompt: Which of the four VASP input files holds the structure?

options.text: POSCAR
options.why: It lists the cell and where the atoms are.

options.text: KPOINTS
options.why: Tempting because it also describes the crystal, but it sets how the repeating pattern is sampled.

options.text: INCAR
options.why: Tempting because it is the main file, but it holds the settings of the run.

hints: The name hints at positions.
Which file is not about sampling or settings?

prompt: Why does this site never show the contents of a POTCAR?

options.text: It comes under your own VASP licence and the site does not reproduce it
options.why: The site never generates or hosts POTCAR content.

options.text: It is always empty
options.why: Tempting because you cannot see it here, but a real POTCAR is not empty.

options.text: The browser cannot display it
options.why: Tempting because it is technical, but the reason is the licence.

hints: Think about who owns it.
The page says you get it under your own licence.
